title: Ford Motor GC to Law Firms: We Are Outpacing Your AI Adoption
pub: Bloomberg Law — Legal Exchange: Insights & Commentary
author: Steven Croley

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source shifts the focus from direct-to-consumer justice access and downward risk transfer to provider-side competition, scalability and law-firm growth. It aligns with the cluster on continued human direction and verification, but does not address whether unrepresented users can verify outputs, obtain effective remedies or face widening inequality.
qs: AI is a new "entrant" in the market for legal services that is increasingly able to compete with both external and in-house counsel.

Although AI tools require human lawyers to scope issues, supply parameters, and validate outputs, this level of oversight is similar in kind (but often lesser in degree) to managing junior attorneys or outside counsel.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core thesis that agentic AI can reshape legal-service delivery, billing and staffing economics, and materially extends it with a major corporate buyer’s perspective: Ford reports stronger in-house adoption than it observes among outside counsel and plans to reward providers that convert AI into demonstrable net savings. Its claims remain explicitly early and company-specific.
qs: **Third,** as concerns the competition between external and in-house counsel, our internal use of AI for increased productivity so far exceeds what we have seen from external counsel.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account and materially develops its buyer-side dimension through Ford’s reported experience. It argues that company-specific knowledge can advantage in-house AI, reports internal productivity use outpacing observed outside-counsel adoption, and supplies a concrete buyer incentive: rewarding external providers only where AI produces net savings. Its conclusions remain explicitly preliminary and company-specific, consistent with the cluster’s caution about the early evidence base.
qs: Meanwhile, in-house lawyers enjoy superior knowledge of their clients' needs, data sources, processes, and operations, positioning them to develop and continuously update tailored AI tools for their clients' daily business.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

st.an: The source accepts that AI is reshaping legal-service economics rather than merely improving productivity, and materially extends the cluster with buyer-side evidence: Ford reports faster in-house adoption than among outside counsel and intends to reward providers that convert AI efficiencies into net savings. Its claims are qualified as early observations from one company rather than settled market-wide findings.
qs: **Third,** as concerns the competition between external and in-house counsel, our internal use of AI for increased productivity so far exceeds what we have seen from external counsel.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Croley directly supports the buyer-transformation proposition: Ford’s in-house team is using company-specific knowledge to develop tailored AI capabilities, raising expectations for outside counsel and using purchasing power to demand measurable productivity and net savings. He also preserves the cluster’s uncertainty about the eventual allocation of work.
qs: Meanwhile, in-house lawyers enjoy superior knowledge of their clients' needs, data sources, processes, and operations, positioning them to develop and continuously update tailored AI tools for their clients' daily business.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that competitive advantage comes from differentiated delivery, organisational adaptability and company-specific knowledge rather than model access alone. It reinforces the roles of smaller-firm agility, tailored in-house capabilities and buyer demands for measurable net savings, while treating outcomes as uncertain; it does not directly develop the build-versus-buy portfolio framework.
qs: AI legal solutions developed internally may therefore serve company needs with greater continuous fidelity and efficacy, which could be a major structural advantage for in-house legal departments over external legal-service providers.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The source supports the core distinction between AI access and dependable firm integration by requiring human validation and financial, technical and cultural investment. Its claims that proactive adopters will gain business and lower costs are optimistic predictions rather than measured firm-wide productivity or ROI evidence, so they do not overturn the cluster’s caution.
qs: Although AI tools require human lawyers to scope issues, supply parameters, and validate outputs, this level of oversight is similar in kind (but often lesser in degree) to managing junior attorneys or outside counsel.
Those who make the right investments—those that are simultaneously financial, technical, and cultural—will gain a larger book of business.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central claim that AI can decouple legal output from lawyer time, pressure billable-hour economics and alter staffing structures. It also reinforces the role of corporate clients and in-house teams in driving adoption, while retaining human validation. Its claims about lower-cost scaling, competitive gains and capacity growth without added headcount are predictive rather than measured, and it does not address the apprenticeship risk in depth.
qs: AI agents operate without the constraints of the billable hour, fundamentally decoupling the time spent on a task from the market value of the output.
They can restructure their organizational charts to integrate agents and dramatically increase capacity without increasing headcount.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central account of AI as workflow reconfiguration rather than wholesale lawyer replacement: it describes broad productivity and capacity gains while retaining human scoping and validation. It also reinforces the cluster’s commercial themes through buyer-side evidence of stronger in-house adoption, pressure on outside counsel and uncertain effects on pricing and market structure. Its claims are more bullish than the synthesis about AI’s quality and sophistication, and it does not engage the apprenticeship risk, but these are limitations rather than substantive opposition.
qs: Although AI tools require human lawyers to scope issues, supply parameters, and validate outputs, this level of oversight is similar in kind (but often lesser in degree) to managing junior attorneys or outside counsel.
**Third,** as concerns the competition between external and in-house counsel, our internal use of AI for increased productivity so far exceeds what we have seen from external counsel.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Croley supports the cluster’s proposition that AI is reshaping legal-service delivery and bargaining between corporate legal departments and outside counsel. Ford’s reported internal lead, potential in-house structural advantage, and commitment to reward firms that produce net savings reinforce the shift, while his acknowledgment of uncertainty aligns with the cluster’s caution that market-wide reallocation and pricing change remain unsettled.
qs: AI will bring a new balance of work between outside counsel and in-house legal departments.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source strongly supports the cluster’s proposition that AI is reshaping legal-service production and economics rather than eliminating lawyers. It links AI to pressure on billable-hour and pyramid economics, requires human validation, and identifies in-house adoption and purchasing pressure as catalysts for reallocating work. Its claims about capability and market effects are more bullish than the synthesis, but it acknowledges uncertainty about the eventual competitive structure.
qs: AI agents operate without the constraints of the billable hour, fundamentally decoupling the time spent on a task from the market value of the output.

Although AI tools require human lawyers to scope issues, supply parameters, and validate outputs, this level of oversight is similar in kind (but often lesser in degree) to managing junior attorneys or outside counsel.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that AI can substitute for substantial legal tasks while complementing lawyers through human scoping and verification, and that this combination may reshape staffing and delivery models. Its prediction that firms can expand capacity without adding headcount is consistent with staffing change despite retained lawyer oversight, although its claims are qualitative forecasts rather than measured employment outcomes.
qs: Although AI tools require human lawyers to scope issues, supply parameters, and validate outputs, this level of oversight is similar in kind (but often lesser in degree) to managing junior attorneys or outside counsel.
They can restructure their organizational charts to integrate agents and dramatically increase capacity without increasing headcount.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI shifts legal-service value from lawyer hours toward integrated technology, organisational capability and client-owned infrastructure. It predicts stronger in-house value capture, pressure on outside counsel to demonstrate net savings, and advantages for firms able to redesign delivery, while acknowledging that these are early observations and the market outcome remains uncertain.
qs: AI agents operate without the constraints of the billable hour, fundamentally decoupling the time spent on a task from the market value of the output.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

kp.k: AI introduces a third legal-service delivery option
kp.d: Croley frames AI as a potential surrogate legal service provider competing with both external counsel and in-house teams, rather than merely a tool. He predicts a redistribution of work between these providers while expressly acknowledging uncertainty about which will harness AI most effectively.
qs: What isn't yet clear is whether external counsel or corporate in-house teams will harness AI most effectively—not just as a tool but as a surrogate legal service provider.
AI will bring a new balance of work between outside counsel and in-house legal departments.

kp.k: Sourcing decisions balance expertise, cost and managerial oversight
kp.d: Croley describes the existing allocation of legal work as depending on relative talent and costs, including quality-control oversight. In-house counsel benefit from company knowledge and easier supervision, whereas external counsel remain attractive for specialized, consequential work that does not recur. This is his framework for understanding how AI changes sourcing decisions.
qs: It's a balance traditionally determined by relative talent and relative cost, where cost includes both compensation and the indirect cost of managerial oversight for quality control.
External counsel can be desirable, even at greater short-term costs, for highly specialized and consequential yet non-recurrent legal work.

kp.k: AI capabilities extend across complex legal tasks
kp.d: Croley asserts that large language models and integrated products can perform complex research, legal problem-solving and composition with superior speed and increasingly high quality. He also argues that model advances make agents attractive across multiple workflows and that AI largely replaces the law library. These are qualitative capability claims, not reported benchmark findings.
qs: Large language models and the products that integrate them undertake complex research tasks, advanced legal problem-solving, and sophisticated composition.
They do so at superior speed and with increasingly exceptional quality.
Advancements in model development make deploying AI agents across multiple workflows attractive and cost-effective.
AI largely replaces the law library, also at low cost, and isn't limited to certain practice areas.

kp.k: Agents decouple task time from output value
kp.d: Croley argues that agents challenge hourly economics because their output is not constrained by billable hours and can scale without a corresponding increase in cost. He presents this as a structural efficiency mechanism, without quantifying costs or specifying a replacement fee arrangement.
qs: AI agents operate without the constraints of the billable hour, fundamentally decoupling the time spent on a task from the market value of the output.
What's more, AI models scale their output without a corresponding increase in cost.

kp.k: Human direction and verification remain necessary
kp.d: Croley conditions AI's effectiveness on lawyers scoping issues, supplying parameters and validating outputs. He likens this oversight to supervising junior lawyers or outside counsel, asserting that it is often less extensive. His descriptions of AI as a super associate and increasingly a super partner concern capability amplification under human direction.
qs: Although AI tools require human lawyers to scope issues, supply parameters, and validate outputs, this level of oversight is similar in kind (but often lesser in degree) to managing junior attorneys or outside counsel.
When properly directed, AI effectively functions as a highly efficient "super associate" and increasingly a "super partner," amplifying the capabilities of both external and in-house legal teams.

kp.k: Adoption requires financial, technical and cultural investment
kp.d: Croley predicts that innovative external counsel will win more business by improving work and lowering costs. He identifies financial, technical and cultural investment as jointly necessary and argues that firms' traditional advantages in anticipating client needs and spreading practices increasingly require proactive AI deployment.
qs: For external counsel, innovative adopters of AI will be well positioned to provide their corporate clients with improved work at lower cost.
Those who make the right investments—those that are simultaneously financial, technical, and cultural—will gain a larger book of business.
Law firms traditionally excel at anticipating their clients' needs and spreading best practices among their wide client base; this seems increasingly unrealistic without proactive deployment of AI.

kp.k: Smaller firms may challenge Big Law's structural advantages
kp.d: Croley suggests that smaller firms' agility and weaker dependence on pyramid economics could facilitate agent integration and capacity growth without additional headcount. He speculates that AI may diminish Big Law's economies of scale and one-stop service advantages; he does not report observed staffing reductions.
qs: Smaller firms, with the ability to pivot quickly, might enjoy some advantage here.
They can restructure their organizational charts to integrate agents and dramatically increase capacity without increasing headcount.

Smaller firms are also less beholden to the pyramid economics that underpin Big Law's profit model—and Big Law's historical advantages associated with economies of scale and the ability to provide "one stop" legal services may become somewhat smaller in an AI world.

kp.k: Client proximity could advantage in-house AI development
kp.d: Croley argues that in-house lawyers' knowledge of company needs, data, processes and operations enables tailored, continuously updated AI tools. He presents superior fit with daily business needs as a possible structural advantage over external providers, rather than an established comparative finding.
qs: Meanwhile, in-house lawyers enjoy superior knowledge of their clients' needs, data sources, processes, and operations, positioning them to develop and continuously update tailored AI tools for their clients' daily business.

AI legal solutions developed internally may therefore serve company needs with greater continuous fidelity and efficacy, which could be a major structural advantage for in-house legal departments over external legal-service providers.

kp.k: Outside counsel adoption appears slow from Ford's perspective
kp.d: Writing in June 2026, Croley characterizes law firms' competitive response as slow despite potential early-mover rewards. He explicitly frames these takeaways from the vantage point of one large public company, not as results of an industry-wide adoption study.
qs: We don't know for sure how this competition in the market for legal services will play out.
But from the vantage point of one large public company, here are some early takeaways.
the competition among outside counsel to harness the advantages of AI seems off to a slow start, especially given the potential rewards for early movers.

kp.k: AI efficiencies have not clearly produced rate relief
kp.d: Croley questions whether AI is delivering genuine outside-counsel rate relief and asserts that most public companies still face standard annual rate increases with little explanation connecting them to future AI efficiencies. He says Ford will reward AI-enabled net savings in the coming months; no rate or savings figures are supplied.
qs: it isn't yet clear how AI will translate into genuine rate relief from outside counsel.
Most public companies continue to see standard annual rate hikes, with little to no explanation for how higher yearly rates reflect investments in law-firm infrastructure for future AI efficiencies.
In the coming months, however, we will look for—and reward—entrepreneurial approaches by external counsel both big and small to meet Ford's legal needs with AI that brings net savings.

kp.k: Ford reports broader, faster internal AI deployment
kp.d: Croley reports that Ford uses AI across all its legal practice areas and that its internal productivity-oriented use exceeds what it has seen from external counsel. He attributes new delivery possibilities to agents but offers client proximity and stronger cost-management motivation only as possible explanations. This is a firsthand qualitative account without quantified productivity comparisons.
qs: our internal use of AI for increased productivity so far exceeds what we have seen from external counsel.
We now employ AI across the full spectrum of our legal practice areas.
AI agents make entirely new legal service delivery models possible, empowering us to leverage our legal capacities dramatically.
Perhaps the advantage of our proximity to the corporate client is just too great for outside lawyers to match, or, maybe we are just more motivated to manage costs.

kp.k: Ford intends to redirect work toward AI innovators
kp.d: Croley commits to further in-house AI investment while inviting external innovation and expressing willingness to pay for demonstrable productivity gains. He forecasts expanding relationships with fast-moving external partners and reducing reliance on laggards, making AI performance a prospective criterion for allocating legal work.
qs: Regardless, we will continue to invest and expand our AI capabilities in-house, even as we solicit innovation from external legal service providers and are prepared to pay for demonstrable gains in productivity.
We are likely to expand our relationships with external partners who innovate and deliver quickly, and curtail our reliance on those who lag behind.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Steven Croley claims that AI is becoming a competing legal-service provider, changing delivery economics and the allocation of work between firms and in-house teams; he predicts commercial rewards for firms that deliver demonstrable AI productivity gains.
pts.d: Croley describes AI as capable of complex research, legal problem-solving and composition at superior speed and increasingly high quality. He claims agents decouple task time from output value, scale output without a corresponding cost increase and largely replace the law library. His surrogate-provider framing still requires human lawyers to define issues, set parameters and verify outputs; he compares that supervision to managing junior lawyers or outside counsel, often with less oversight. He predicts that firms making financial, technical and cultural investments will deliver better work at lower cost and win more business. Smaller firms may increase capacity without increasing headcount, while their flexibility and lesser dependence on pyramid economics could diminish Big Law's scale and one-stop-service advantages. In-house teams may gain a structural advantage through client-specific knowledge and tailored AI tools. Croley reports that Ford's internal AI productivity use exceeds what it has seen from outside counsel, while external adoption appears slow and rate relief remains unclear. Ford intends to expand relationships with rapid innovators and reduce reliance on laggards.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on Croley's experience as Ford's general counsel, reported internal adoption and observations of outside counsel, supplemented by qualitative economic reasoning rather than quantitative evaluations.
pts.d: Croley reports that Ford uses AI across all its legal practice areas and that its internal use for productivity exceeds what it has observed externally. He also reports continuing annual outside-counsel rate increases without clear explanations linking those increases to future AI efficiencies. His predictions about competitive advantage derive from differences in client proximity, organizational flexibility, staffing economics and the ability to spread practices across clients. The article supplies no measured productivity gains, cost comparisons, model benchmarks, named deployments or supporting datasets. Statements about superior output quality, lower supervisory requirements and future market shares are presented as his assessments or predictions, not demonstrated comparative findings. Ford's stated procurement intentions provide a concrete buyer-side signal, not evidence that the predicted market-wide reallocation has already occurred.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing on 22 June 2026, Croley portrays disruption as underway, anticipates imminent rapid change and identifies the coming months as Ford's window for rewarding AI-driven net savings.
pts.d: Current-tense claims concern AI capabilities, Ford's adoption across practice areas, perceived external-counsel lag and the absence of clear rate relief. Future predictions concern a new balance of work, changing competitive advantages and business gains for effective adopters, without a fixed market-wide deadline. Ford specifically plans to seek and reward net savings in the coming months and to continue expanding internal capabilities. Claimed benefits depend on proper human direction and verification, appropriate financial, technical and cultural investments, and demonstrable productivity gains. Croley qualifies smaller-firm and in-house advantages as possibilities and explicitly leaves the ultimate outcome of competition unresolved. His suggestions that client proximity or stronger cost motivation explain Ford's lead are hypotheses rather than established causes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern corporate legal services, especially large public-company buyers, their in-house teams and competing outside law firms of different sizes.
pts.d: Ford and other large corporate clients are positioned to demand productivity improvements and net savings and to redirect external spend. In-house lawyers may expand delivery capacity through company-specific tools while retaining issue scoping and output verification. Outside firms face both opportunities to win business and the risk of losing relationships if adoption lags. Smaller firms may expand capacity without additional headcount; Big Law may face pressure on its pyramid-based profit model and historical scale advantages. Junior lawyers appear as a comparator for AI's work and supervision, but Croley makes no quantified employment or layoff prediction. The article does not make claims about unmet civil legal need or access to justice.
